market_context: United States/international; cooked fish and drained canned fish
title: Highest-Protein Fish: Ranking Per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Fish per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Compare tuna, sardines, cod, salmon, mackerel and lean white fish by protein per 100 grams, with context on omega-3 and mercury.
seo.search_intent: Rank fish by protein density while preserving broader nutrition context.

excerpt: Tuna is near 29 g of protein per 100 g, but sardines, mackerel, trout, cod and salmon are also highly concentrated sources. The comparison keeps preparation simple—cooked or canned—and explains separately how water, fat, sodium and mercury affect the bigger picture.
content_html:
Fish is generally a very concentrated source of protein. Most common choices provide roughly 20 to 30 grams of protein per 100 grams once cooked or, for canned fish, drained.

To keep the comparison useful, this article does not turn every cooking method into a separate ranking. Fresh fish is shown simply as cooked, while canned fish is shown drained. Grilling, baking, steaming or pan-cooking can shift the number slightly because they change water content, but they do not transform an ordinary fish into a completely different protein food.

Simple protein ranking per 100 grams

FishForm comparedApprox. proteinApprox. calories
TunaCooked29 g130 kcal
AnchoviesCanned, drained29 g210 kcal
SardinesCanned, drained25 g208 kcal
MackerelCooked24 g262 kcal
TroutCooked24 g168 kcal
SwordfishCooked23 g172 kcal
CodCooked23 g105 kcal
SalmonCooked22 g206 kcal

The figures are rounded from USDA FoodData Central references. Rounding is intentional: tenths of a gram are not very useful when the real value also varies with species, cut and the amount of water lost during cooking.

Tuna: a lot of protein for relatively few calories

The cooked tuna reference used here provides about 29 g of protein and 130 calories per 100 g. That makes it highly protein-dense.

It is not automatically the fish to eat most often. Some tuna species are large predators and can accumulate more mercury than smaller fish. Frequency therefore depends on the type of tuna, the variety of fish in the diet and, for people who are pregnant or may become pregnant and for children, current FDA/EPA fish guidance.

Anchovies and sardines: concentrated, but portions are usually smaller

Canned anchovies provide about 29 g of protein per 100 g, while sardines provide about 25 g. A 100 g serving of anchovies, however, is much larger than most people normally eat.

Canned fish also needs context. Anchovies can be very high in sodium; sardines with edible bones provide calcium; and oil-packed products carry more calories even after some of the oil is drained.

Mackerel, trout and salmon: high protein with more fat

Mackerel, trout and salmon remain high-protein fish at roughly 22–24 g per 100 g in these references. The bigger difference from cod or very lean tuna is fat.

Cooked cod is about 105 calories per 100 g, compared with roughly 206 calories for salmon and 262 for mackerel. Salmon and mackerel also provide substantial EPA and DHA omega-3 fats.

Cod: similar protein with very little fat

Cooked cod provides about 23 g of protein and 105 calories per 100 g. Compared with salmon, the protein is almost the same—23 versus 22 g—but the calories are roughly half because cod is much leaner.

Salt cod is a different comparison because curing dramatically changes sodium and also changes water content.

What if you eat fish raw, such as sushi or sashimi?

Raw fish usually contains a little more water than the same fish after cooking. It can therefore show less protein per 100 g, even though cooking has not created protein; water has simply been lost and the nutrients are more concentrated by weight.

If you are comparing two sashimi choices, use raw values for both. For a general ranking, cooked fish and drained canned fish better reflect the usual form in which these foods are eaten without mixing states silently.

Does white fish have less protein than oily fish?

Not necessarily. Cod in this comparison provides about 23 g per 100 g, while salmon provides about 22 g and mackerel about 24 g. The clearest difference between lean and oily fish is usually fat, not protein.

Protein per serving

ExampleServingApprox. protein
Cooked tuna150 g44 g
Cooked trout150 g36 g
Cooked cod150 g34 g
Cooked salmon150 g33 g
Canned sardines100 g25 g

A difference between 22 and 24 g per 100 g is small in a normal meal. Once you know these are all strong protein sources, taste, variety, omega-3 content, sodium, calcium, fat and species-specific safety guidance become more useful tie-breakers.

Bottom line

If protein concentration is the only metric, tuna and anchovies sit near the top at about 29 g per 100 g. Sardines, mackerel, trout, swordfish, cod and salmon are also high, generally around 22–25 g.

The useful conclusion is not that one species wins. Most of these fish do the protein job extremely well; the more meaningful differences come from the rest of their nutrition profile and from eating a variety of species.

Sources and method

Values are rounded from USDA FoodData Central and the composition references already listed in the article sources. The table uses only two reader-friendly states—cooked fish and drained canned fish—and explains separately when preparation mainly changes water, sodium or calories.

faq.question: Which fish has the most protein?
faq.answer: In the references compared here, cooked tuna and canned anchovies are around 29 g per 100 g. Sardines, mackerel, trout, swordfish, cod and salmon are generally around 22–25 g.

faq.question: Does salmon have less protein than tuna?
faq.answer: In these references, yes: about 22 g/100 g for salmon versus 29 g/100 g for tuna. Salmon also contains more fat and long-chain omega-3s, so protein is only one part of the comparison.

faq.question: Does grilling or baking change the protein number?
faq.answer: It can shift the value slightly by changing water content. Cooking does not create protein; losing moisture simply concentrates protein per 100 g.

faq.question: Does white fish have less protein?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Cooked cod is around 23 g/100 g, very similar to many oily fish. Fat content usually differs more than protein.
